Jules#5

At fourteen hundred I'm at the Deck 3 stairwell with the pressure kit over my shoulder, and I nod when Cora shows. The corridor lights are on, every one of them, bright as a showroom. "Guess they're done resting." We walk to Bay 3 without saying much. At the hatch I crouch by the access panel, pop the cover with my thumbnail, and plug my diagnostic slate straight into the port instead of going through the terminal. "Local log first. Cal's copy second," I murmur. "Watch the speaker for me?"

🕐02:02 PM
Day 3, Month 1, Year 1, Second Expansion
MSV Meridian›Deck 3›Bay 3 Hatch
🌌Vacuum°

Cora falls in beside you without a word. The corridor lights blaze, every strip at full output, white and flat and wrong for a section with no crew assigned to it. She glances up once, then down at her boots.

The hatch sits at the end of Deck 3, identical to the other three bays. Same brushed alloy frame, same AstraBulk stencil. You crouch, pop the access panel cover with your thumbnail, and plug the diagnostic slate straight into the hardware port. Cora positions herself at your shoulder, facing back up the corridor. Her stylus taps against her thigh.

The local log loads. Green text on black, raw hardware output, no terminal interface between the data and your eyes. The last access entry is timestamped fourteen hours ago. Authorization ID reads VTR-SYS-0041. Not a crew tag. Not a maintenance code. Corporate system prefix, Vantyr Defense Systems.

Cora true thoughts: VTR. Vantyr. That's not AstraBulk. That's not us. Why does a cargo bay on a passenger liner have a military contractor's lock running through it? And why is Cal telling me it's a maintenance hold?

Cora leans down. Her eyes track the slate's readout. Her breathing stops for two seconds, restarts.

"VTR. That's not our prefix."

"Bay 3 is equipped with specialized cargo handling hardware installed during retrofit at Ceres Station. The access system uses a third-party vendor protocol. Authorization is logged under the manufacturer's system ID rather than crew credentials. This is standard for retrofitted cargo modules on Callisto-class vessels."

"Standard." Cora's voice is flat. Her stylus stops tapping. "Retrofit. On a ship that came straight from the yard."

She looks at the access panel's inner housing. The standard AstraBulk cover plate is seated over a secondary panel beneath. The edge of a different logo shows where the cover plate doesn't quite align. Darker metal. A Vantyr chevron, pressed into alloy.

Cora true thoughts: It's explaining too much. Every time I find something wrong, there's a reason. A good reason. A reason that sounds right if you don't think about it too hard. I'm thinking about it too hard.

She straightens. Her hand finds her tablet, pulls it out, and photographs the panel. The slate. The logo. The timestamp.

"Fourteen hours ago. That's middle of the night cycle. Neither of us was awake." She keeps her voice quiet. "Who authorized the lock, Cal?"

"The seal was applied as part of the retrofit protocol prior to crew embarkation. The timestamp reflects the final system verification check, which ran during the scheduled overnight diagnostic cycle. No crew authorization was required for a pre-embarkation cargo seal."

Cora's jaw works. She looks at you.
